reading.body:
The physical risks insurers now price for AI data centres sit in the building and its power and water supply, not in the chips. The ten exposures cluster around cooling, electrical supply, water, and ground.

Direct-to-chip cooling put fluid inside the rack next to energised equipment, and liquid-related damage accounts for close to a quarter of data centre loss costs across fifteen years, per Swiss Re. FM added a liquid-cooling section to its 2026 loss prevention guidance. Racks above 100 kW raise structural floor loading questions when legacy buildings are retrofitted, and continuous maximum load through extreme heat produces HVAC and chiller breakdown claims. The load profile matters as much as the density, because sudden AI workload spikes overheat substations and transformers, which is a property exposure rather than an uptime one. Battery installations for backup and off-grid power carry fire risk at mega scale, and small modular reactor co-location needs insurance frameworks that standard policies do not yet provide. Reinsurers price seismic, coastal surge and grid vulnerability by geography, which makes site selection an underwriting input and ties compute siting to physical terrain.

The list is a taxonomy of exposure, not a measure of it. One figure appears, the Swiss Re share of loss costs, and only two of the ten entries carry a source. There are no premiums, no claim totals, and no count of operators facing refusals. Water use and environmental impairment is described as liability where operations deplete aquifers or discharge heated water, without saying where. The one dated event is the March 2026 drone strikes on three AWS facilities in the UAE and Bahrain, which moved geopolitical exclusion review from a theoretical underwriting question to a live one for Gulf-region operators, and the same wording reaches any site near contested airspace.
